summary: An early draft of requirements for IP routers, meant to replace RFC 1009 on Internet gateways. It defines and discusses requirements for devices that forward packets at the network layer. It was replaced by RFC 1812.

eli5.summary: A checklist of what a good internet traffic-director device must do.

subtitle: Comprehensive IP router design and operational requirements

tldr.problem: Routers performing IP forwarding lacked a unified specification; implementations varied widely, causing interoperability problems and inconsistent behavior across the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: A detailed requirements document covering all layers of the Internet protocol stack, specifying how routers must handle addressing, packet forwarding, routing protocols, error messages, and network management.
tldr.outcome: Provided a standard template for router behavior to promote interoperability, though was itself superseded by RFC 1812 which provided similar requirements with updates.

facts.label: Major router functions
facts.value: Forwarding, routing, error reporting, network management

today: RFC 1812 superseded RFC 1716 in June 1995, providing an updated set of IP router requirements. RFC 1716 is now Historic status and is no longer the current standard, though it remains a valuable reference for understanding early Internet routing architecture and the evolution of router specifications.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1716 aimed to replace RFC 1009 with a comprehensive specification for IP routers—devices that examine IP addresses and forward packets between networks. Routers form the backbone of the Internet by relaying datagrams from source to destination across multiple hops.

The RFC recognizes that routers are fundamentally different from hosts: while hosts can originate and receive data, routers must also forward packets that are destined for other systems. A router examines each packet's IP header, decides where to send it next based on the destination address, modifies the header as needed, and replaces the link-layer framing for transmission on the output network.

This document enumerates protocols that Internet-connected routers must implement, corrects errors in existing specifications, and provides explicit requirements for handling edge cases and error conditions. The document emphasizes that router vendors often implement extensions or workarounds for compatibility with non-compliant systems already deployed in the Internet, but these requirements represent the ideal standard toward which the Internet should move.
sections.eli5: The RFC is an instruction manual for building Internet routers. It says what rules routers must follow, which languages they must speak, and how they must treat packets that arrive with unusual problems.

sections.title: Internet Architecture and Router Role
sections.content:
The Internet uses a layered protocol architecture. At the bottom sits the Link Layer, which handles direct connections over Ethernet, PPP, or other physical networks. Above that is the Internet Layer, where IP provides unreliable, connectionless datagram transport. The Transport Layer (TCP and UDP) adds reliability or demultiplexing as needed. Application protocols (DNS, HTTP, SMTP) sit at the top.

Within this architecture, routers sit at the Internet Layer boundary. A router connects two or more networks and appears as a connected host on each one, with its own IP address(es). Routers receive packets from connected networks, examine the destination IP address, consult a routing table (also called a forwarding table), and decide which output interface should receive the packet for the next hop toward the destination.

Routers operate within autonomous systems (ASs)—administrative domains like an ISP or company network. Within an AS, routers run an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) like OSPF or RIP to share routing information with each other. Between ASs, routers run an Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) like BGP to exchange topology information. This hierarchical approach allows the Internet to scale: routers outside an AS need only know how to reach the AS as a whole, not every subnet inside it.

Unlike bridges (which operate at the Link Layer) or hosts (which do not forward), routers are the active forwarding elements that keep packets moving across network boundaries.
sections.eli5: Routers are the traffic directors of the Internet. They stand at the borders between networks, look at each packet's destination address, and decide which path it should take next. Routers share route information with each other to keep their routing tables up to date.

sections.title: Link Layer Interfaces and Network Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how routers must interact with the hardware links that connect them to networks. Each router has physical interfaces that connect to Ethernet, serial lines, ATM, Frame Relay, or other media. Each interface must have a way to determine whether it is operational, and the router must be able to detect when an interface fails or recovers.

For local-area networks like Ethernet, routers must implement the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), which maps IP addresses to MAC addresses (hardware identifiers). When a router needs to send a packet to a neighbor, ARP allows it to discover the neighbor's hardware address.

For serial point-to-point links (like those connecting routers across long distances), routers MUST implement Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP). PPP negotiates parameters such as the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU), link quality monitoring, and optional compression. Routers on slow serial links (19.2 kbps or less) SHOULD perform Van Jacobson header compression to reduce bandwidth consumption.

The RFC also covers Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) negotiation and handling. Different networks have different MTUs (Ethernet uses 1,500 bytes, while some networks use smaller values). Routers must handle packets of varying sizes and know how to fragment large packets that exceed an outgoing interface's MTU.

All interfaces must support the ability to detect failures through mechanisms like link-state monitoring or echo requests. When an interface goes down, the router must immediately withdraw routes that depend on it to prevent black holes.
sections.eli5: Routers need to talk to many kinds of networks. The RFC says which connection types routers must support (like Ethernet and PPP) and how they must detect if a connection is broken. Routers also need to ask 'what is the hardware address of that IP address?' using ARP.

sections.title: Internet Layer: IP, ICMP, and IGMP
sections.content:
The core of Internet routing is the Internet Protocol (IP), defined in RFC 791 and updated with subnetting (RFC 950) and broadcast (RFC 919) extensions. RFC 1716 clarifies how routers must handle IP options—such as source routing, record route, and timestamps—that senders can embed in packet headers.

A key requirement is that routers MUST NOT discard a packet merely because it contains an unknown or reserved bit, since future protocol versions may use those bits. Similarly, if a packet contains IP options that the router does not understand, the router must preserve them unchanged and forward them to the next hop.

The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is how routers signal errors and exchange control information. When a router cannot forward a packet (e.g., no route exists, or the TTL is exhausted), it MUST send an ICMP Destination Unreachable or Time Exceeded message back to the source. ICMP also carries echo requests and replies (the basis of the ping utility) and router discovery messages that help hosts find routers on their local network.

A critical rule: routers MUST NOT send ICMP error messages in response to broadcast or multicast packets, or in response to other ICMP error messages. This prevents broadcast storms—cascading floods of error messages that can cripple a network. Rate limiting of ICMP messages is also essential.

The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) allows hosts to join and leave multicast groups. A multicast-aware router SHOULD implement IGMP to learn which hosts on its local network are interested in which multicast addresses, so it can forward multicast traffic only to interfaces where interested hosts exist.
sections.eli5: IP is how packets are addressed and routed. ICMP is the error messenger: if something goes wrong (no route found, TTL expired), ICMP tells the sender. IGMP is how routers learn which hosts want to receive each multicast channel. The RFC says routers must handle all these correctly and not send too many error messages.

sections.title: Packet Forwarding Algorithm
sections.content:
The core of router operation is the forwarding process—the algorithm that processes each arriving packet. The RFC describes this in detail because no single IP specification fully covers it.

When a packet arrives, the router first validates the IP header: the version must be 4, the header length must be reasonable, the total length must match the actual packet size, and the checksum must be correct. Any packet that fails these checks is silently discarded; the router may log the error but does not send ICMP messages for invalid headers (to avoid amplifying problems).

Next, the router processes IP options that can be handled before routing, such as source routes. If the packet contains a source route option that names the router as a hop, the router inserts its own address and advances the pointer in the option.

The router then decides whether the packet is destined for itself or for another system. Packets destined for the router are delivered locally to the appropriate transport protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP, etc.). All other packets (and sometimes certain broadcasts and multicasts) are queued for forwarding.

For unicast packets being forwarded, the router performs these steps: (1) looks up the destination IP address in the routing table to find the best-matching route and determine the output interface; (2) verifies that forwarding is permitted by checking source and destination address validity and any access control lists; (3) decrements the Time-to-Live (TTL) field and discards the packet if TTL reaches zero, sending an ICMP Time Exceeded message; (4) processes any remaining IP options; (5) fragments the packet if necessary for the output interface's MTU; (6) resolves the next-hop address to a hardware address using ARP; (7) encapsulates the packet in a link-layer frame and queues it for transmission; and (8) optionally sends an ICMP Redirect message to the packet's source if appropriate.

For multicast packets, the algorithm differs: the router checks that the packet arrived on the expected interface (using reverse path forwarding), then forwards copies out multiple interfaces based on multicast routing state, using link-layer multicast encapsulation rather than unicast.

This algorithm is presented in a simplified form. Implementors optimize it for throughput and use various data structures (tries, hash tables, etc.) to achieve wire-speed forwarding, as long as the result is equivalent.
sections.eli5: When a packet arrives, the router checks if it's broken (bad checksum, wrong version). If it's for the router itself, the router keeps it. Otherwise, the router looks up where to send it next, decrements the hop-limit counter, and passes it to the right output link. If the hop-limit reaches zero, the router sends an error message back.

sections.title: Routing Protocols and Information Exchange
sections.content:
Routers alone cannot forward packets without knowing where to send them. Routing protocols allow routers to learn about network topology from each other and build their routing tables dynamically.

Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) operate within a single autonomous system. The RFC discusses three major IGPs. RIP (Routing Information Protocol) is the oldest and simplest: routers advertise reachability to all destinations, with path costs equal to hop counts (distance). RIP is easy to implement but scales poorly (hop count limit of 15). OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) builds a complete map of the network and uses sophisticated algorithms to find the best path; it scales much better. IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is similar to OSPF but originated in the OSI world.

Exterior Gateway Protocols (EGPs) exchange routing information between autonomous systems. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the standard EGP; it allows each AS to advertise reachability to networks within that AS and to learn reachability to other ASs. BGP is policy-based: an AS can choose which routes to advertise, which routes to accept, and how to prefer one path over another based on business relationships.

The RFC specifies requirements for how routers must handle learned routes: routes received from an IGP are used for forwarding; routes learned via ICMP Redirects are generally not trusted by modern routers (since they might be forged). Routers SHOULD validate routes received from other routers to prevent accepting obviously incorrect information (such as routes claiming to reach the source router from the source router itself).

Routers may also use static routing, where an administrator manually configures routes. Static routing is common in small networks or as a fallback mechanism.
sections.eli5: Routers talk to each other using routing protocols to share maps of the network. Inside one organization, routers might use OSPF or RIP to learn routes to each other. Between organizations, they use BGP. This way, each router knows how to reach every network in the Internet.

sections.title: Network Management and Operations
sections.content:
Operating a router requires configuration, monitoring, and maintenance. The RFC specifies requirements for network management, which allows operators to monitor and control routers remotely.

The standard tool is the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), which allows management stations to query routers for statistics (packet counts, interface status, routing table entries) and to modify configuration. Routers must support SNMP and populate standard Management Information Bases (MIBs) that define the objects an operator can read and modify.

Routers must support BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol) and TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) for booting from a network server. This allows a router to obtain its initial configuration and software from a central location without requiring manual setup on each device.

The RFC emphasizes the importance of error logging. Routers should log unusual events (malformed packets, unexpected ICMP messages, interface failures) in a way that helps operators diagnose problems. However, logging must be carefully designed: circular buffers can prevent logs from filling the router's memory, and filtering can prevent duplicate messages from overwhelming the operator.

Routers need configuration options for many parameters, including which protocols to enable, which routes to accept, and how to behave in edge cases. The RFC recognizes that perfect, fully self-configuring routers are impossible: administrators must understand their network and configure routers accordingly. However, reasonable defaults—such as requiring routers to come up without routing enabled until explicitly configured—prevent misconfigured routers from damaging the network.

The RFC also specifies that routers must support out-of-band management—the ability to manage a failed router through a separate console connection or dial-up modem, independent of the router's normal IP forwarding path.
sections.eli5: Routers need to be managed remotely. SNMP is the tool operators use to check router status, see statistics, and change settings. Routers also need to be able to boot from a server and log errors for troubleshooting.

sections.title: Robustness, Error Handling, and Configuration
sections.content:
The RFC is deeply concerned with making routers robust in the face of errors, misconfiguration, and malicious or broken peer systems. This reflects lessons learned from operating a large, heterogeneous network where any given router might encounter packets or behavior from systems written long ago, modified locally, or deliberately hostile.

The Robustness Principle states: be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others. In practice, this means a router should be strict about its own behavior (send well-formed packets, follow protocols exactly) but very tolerant of packets it receives. A router MUST ignore reserved bits in headers, must not break on unrecognized protocol values, and must survive in the presence of misbehaving hosts.

The RFC specifies detailed error handling for every major protocol. For example, when the TTL field reaches zero during forwarding, the router MUST send an ICMP Time Exceeded message (which traceroute uses). When source routing fails, the router sends a Destination Unreachable message with code Source Route Failed.

Type of Service (TOS) handling allows routers to treat packets differently based on service class. The RFC requires routers to consider the TOS field when selecting routes; some paths may be optimized for low delay, others for high throughput. This allows operators to configure different treatment for interactive (low-delay) vs. bulk (high-throughput) traffic.

Routers must implement Martian address filtering: silently discarding packets with obviously invalid source addresses (such as 0.0.0.0, broadcast addresses, or multicast sources), preventing these packets from causing problems downstream.

Access control lists (packet filtering) allow routers to drop or pass packets based on source address, destination address, protocol, and port. This enables administrators to implement basic firewalls and security policies.

The RFC notes that configuration is inherently complex: a router must know its own IP addresses and subnet masks, must be able to learn routes from neighbors, and must respect administrative settings. The document strongly recommends against auto-configuration features that might cause router misconfiguration: a router should not start forwarding until explicitly enabled and configured.
sections.eli5: Routers must be prepared for anything: broken packets, misbehaving neighbors, misconfiguration. The RFC says routers should be strict about their own behavior but tolerant of others. Routers can filter packets, prioritize different kinds of traffic, and log problems to help operators understand what went wrong.
